title: How do microservices maintain sessions when jumping between services (stateless JWT in the Authorization header, each service validates)?
shortTitle: How do microservices maintain sessions when jumping between services
keyPoints: Microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request.
Each service validates the token locally by checking signature, expiry, issuer, and audience.
The token IS the session: identity travels with the request, not stored on any server.
Any instance of any service can handle any request because nothing is stored in instance memory.
Traditional server-side sessions break in microservices because a session in one instance is invisible to others.
The honest tradeoff is revocation: a JWT cannot be easily invalidated; use short-lived access tokens with refresh rotation.
For rare immediate-revocation needs, maintain a small denylist of revoked token IDs.

s1_definition.oneliner: Microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request, and each service validates it locally, so there is no shared session and any instance can serve any request.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Stateless authentication** – The client carries a self-contained signed JWT on every request; no server stores session state.
- **Local validation** – Each service checks the token's signature, expiry, issuer, and audience without calling the identity provider.
- **Token IS the session** – The identity and roles that a traditional session stored on the server now travel inside the signed token.
- **Horizontal scalability** – Any instance of any service handles any request because nothing is in instance memory.
- **Revocation tradeoff** – A self-contained token is valid until expiry; mitigate with short-lived access tokens and refresh rotation.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh visits several departments at National Bank of India during one trip. In the old system, the receptionist keeps a note saying "Rajesh is inside", and every clerk phones the receptionist to confirm, which breaks when there are many branches. Instead the bank gives Rajesh a tamper-proof pass when he proves his identity, and he shows it at every department. Each department reads and verifies the pass itself, with no phone call to anyone.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stateless Session with JWT:

  ┌──────────┐  login  ┌──────────┐
  │  Client  │────────▶│ Auth Svc │  verify credentials
  │ (mobile) │◀────────│          │  mint JWT
  └──────┬───┘  JWT    └──────────┘
         │
         │ Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
         │
    ┌────▼─────┐  validate  ┌──────────────┐
    │ Account  │  JWT       │ Instance 1   │ any instance
    │ Service  │  locally   │ Instance 2   │ serves any
    │          │            │ Instance 3   │ request
    └────┬─────┘            └──────────────┘
         │
         │ Authorization: Bearer <jwt> (same token)
         │
    ┌────▼─────┐  validate
    │ Transfer │  JWT
    │ Service  │  locally
    └──────────┘

  No server-side session anywhere.
  Token carries the identity.
  Any instance, any service.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Microservices do not maintain traditional server-side sessions. Instead, the client carries a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request, and each service validates it locally by checking the signature, expiry, issuer, and audience. The token IS the session: the identity and roles that a server-side session would have stored now travel inside the signed token, so any instance of any service can handle any request.

The traditional model breaks in microservices because a session in one instance's memory is invisible to the others. A load balancer sends the next request to a different instance that has no session, so the user appears logged out. At National Bank of India, Rajesh was frustrated by intermittent logouts until Pankaj switched to stateless JWTs: Rajesh logged in once and was recognized on any instance of any service.

The honest tradeoff is revocation. A self-contained token is valid until it expires, so a stolen token is usable for its remaining lifetime. The mitigation is short-lived access tokens (5 minutes) paired with refresh tokens that are revoked on logout. For cases needing instant revocation, a small denylist of token IDs adds a little shared state back.

Remember one sentence: microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT on every request and each service validate it locally, so there is no shared session, any instance serves any request, and the only tradeoff is revocation handled with short-lived tokens and refresh rotation.
